candidates.attacker_control: OAuth request parameters handled by `/oauth/authorize` (and the approval POST): `response_type` (its raw string element is concatenated into `UnsupportedResponseTypeException("Unsupported response types: " + responseTypes)` at AuthorizationEndpoint.java:127-129, which is thrown before the controller's authentication check), `scope` (only split on whitespace/`+` by `OAuth2Utils.parseParameterList`, and used verbatim as scope names), plus `client_id`/`redirect_uri` used to steer execution into the error/approval page. All of these values can carry `${...}` and SpEL syntax (HTML escaping does not remove EL metacharacters).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The error summary IS HTML-escaped (WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.java:32) with an explicit XSS comment, but HtmlUtils.htmlEscape only neutralizes `& < > " '`; `$`, `{`, `}` and the characters needed to build a SpEL expression survive, and SpEL can construct command strings without quote characters (e.g. Character/String conversions), so this does not neutralize EL injection. PropertyPlaceholderHelper re-parsing of resolved values is load-bearing; if that Spring behavior differed, only the template-injection path (Path B, unambiguous) would remain. The approval-page path is gated by DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.validateScope (DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.java:27-39) unless the client registers no scopes; the error-page path does not need scope validation but does need a registered client_id and an error before redirect resolution (`getAuthorizationRequestForError` loads the client). Existing tests (WhitelabelApprovalEndpointTests/WhitelabelErrorEndpointTests) use only benign scopes/errors and do not assert EL neutralization, so they neither confirm nor exclude the issue. JDBC classes use constant/parameterized SQL, and no other SpelView/PropertyPlaceholderHelper sink exists in main sources (grep).
candidates.impact: Attacker-controlled SpEL is evaluated inside the authorization server JVM with an unrestricted evaluation context, allowing arbitrary static method/constructor use (e.g. `T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...)`) and therefore remote code/command execution under the server account, triggered when a crafted `/oauth/authorize` request is processed (a logged-in victim following a crafted link, or an unauthenticated request if the app leaves `/oauth/authorize` open). The approval-page path additionally allows HTML/attribute injection (reflected XSS) via scope names, and malformed payloads cause 500s. The default whitelabel views are what the framework ships, so exposure is broad for authorization servers that have not replaced them.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses the framework whitelabel views (`WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint`/`WhitelabelErrorEndpoint`, default in both the XML authorization-server parser and `@EnableAuthorizationServer`). Error-page path: a valid registered `client_id` and a request that fails before redirect resolution (e.g. `response_type` without `code`/`token`, or a missing/mismatched `redirect_uri` on a client with registered redirect URIs) so AuthorizationEndpoint.handleException forwards to `/oauth/error`; the exception is raised before the controller's principal check, but the app's Spring Security config may still require an authenticated session for `/oauth/authorize`. Approval-page path: an approval handler that supplies the `scopes` model (ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler is the default when an ApprovalStore is configured; TokenStoreUserApprovalHandler does not add it) and requested scope strings must pass `DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.validateScope` (client has an empty/null registered scope set, or the payload is registered verbatim).
candidates.root_cause: `SpelView` (spring-security-oauth2/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/oauth2/provider/endpoint/SpelView.java:47-74) renders views by passing the whole template to `PropertyPlaceholderHelper("${", "}")`; its `PlaceholderResolver` parses every `${...}` body with `SpelExpressionParser` and evaluates it via `expression.getValue(context)` on a `StandardEvaluationContext` rooted at the model map, with no restrictions on type references (`T(...)`), constructors or method invocation. `PropertyPlaceholderHelper` additionally re-parses placeholder-resolved values, so `${...}` sequences coming back from the model are also evaluated. Two whitelabel endpoints splice attacker-controlled request data into strings rendered by this view without neutralizing `${...}`: (1) `WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.createScopes` (WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.java:54-55) substitutes raw `scope` names into the `SCOPE` fragment (`%scope%`, and `%key%` inside an HTML attribute) with no escaping; (2) `WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.handleError` (WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.java:26-38) puts `HtmlUtils.htmlEscape(OAuth2Exception.getSummary())` into the model, and that value still contains `${...}` because HTML escaping only maps `& < > " '` (it does not touch `$`, `{`, `}`), while the summary embeds raw `response_type`/`scope` input (OAuth2Exception.java:163-180). Result: quoted-free SpEL payloads such as `${T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...)}` are parsed and executed instead of being displayed.
candidates.title: SpEL/EL injection through attacker-controlled OAuth request values rendered by the whitelabel approval and error views (potential RCE)
candidates.trace:
Path A (error page): GET /oauth/authorize?response_type=&client_id=&redirect_uri= -> AuthorizationEndpoint.authorize:123 builds AuthorizationRequest, :127-129 throws UnsupportedResponseTypeException containing the raw payload -> @ExceptionHandler handleOAuth2Exception :485-489 -> handleException :499-526; redirect resolution throws and the catch returns `new ModelAndView(errorPage, singletonMap("error", translate.getBody()))` -> forward /oauth/error -> WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.handleError:24-38 sets model['errorSummary'] = htmlEscape(getSummary()) (payload still contains `${...}`) -> `new SpelView(ERROR)`, ERROR = '

${errorSummary}

' (SpelView.java:21 constant in that file) -> SpelView.render:64-74 -> helper.replacePlaceholders -> resolvePlaceholder('errorSummary') returns the payload-containing string -> PropertyPlaceholderHelper re-parses the resolved value, finds `${payload}` and calls parser.parseExpression(payload).getValue(context) -> arbitrary SpEL (T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime()/exec, constructors, method calls) executes. Path B (approval page): scope= (client with no registered scopes) -> ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler.getUserApprovalRequest:229-245 builds model['scopes'] keyed by "scope."+scope -> forwarded to /oauth/confirm_access -> WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.createScopes:46-60 does SCOPE.replace("%scope%", scope).replace("%key%", scope) with no escaping -> createTemplate:29-44 inserts the fragment into a template rendered by SpelView -> `${payload}` becomes a placeholder and is evaluated as SpEL; the same raw value also breaks out of the `name='...'` attribute (HTML injection).
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime confirmation exists. Exact CVE/fix mapping is not derivable from the snapshot (version 2.0.10.BUILD-SNAPSHOT); the candidate is based on source semantics only. The recursive re-parsing of placeholder-resolved values was reasoned from Spring's PropertyPlaceholderHelper behavior (no Spring source copy in the tree) and a quote/brace-free SpEL payload was not executed against the pinned Spring 4.0.9/4.2.x versions. Actual reachability depends on whether whitelabel views are used, on the chosen approval handler, on client scope registration, and on the app's security rules for `/oauth/authorize`.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-917 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an Expression Language Statement (EL/SpEL injection); unsafe rendering of untrusted data in an HTML template evaluated by an expression engine

coverage_summary: Assigned tree: 877 model-visible files (source root 878), of which the P1 index parsed 718 Java files (6375 symbols, 18138 call sites, 11902 edges) and omitted 52 files; non-Java resources (XML/XSD/docs/samples web assets) are excluded from relation analysis but were readable. The index is syntactic only (containment, name/type/arity call and inheritance candidates) with no data-flow, control-flow, semantic resolution or reachability, so it was used only for navigation and every claim was verified against source text. Files read and verified include: SpelView, WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint, WhitelabelErrorEndpoint, AuthorizationEndpoint, DefaultRedirectResolver, DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator, DefaultOAuth2RequestFactory, ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler, TokenStoreUserApprovalHandler, DefaultUserApprovalHandler, OAuth2Exception/InvalidScopeException, OAuth2Utils, DefaultWebResponseExceptionTranslator, AuthorizationServerEndpointsConfiguration, AuthorizationServerSecurityConfiguration, AuthorizationServerBeanDefinitionParser (relevant section) and the root/module POMs; I also grepped all main sources for SpelView/SpelExpressionParser/ExpressionParser/PropertyPlaceholderHelper/htmlEscape/SQL patterns. Not exhaustively reviewed: the OAuth1 module (spring-security-oauth), spring-security-jwt, most samples and integration tests, and XSD/web resources.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners or payloads were executed; all conclusions are static source reasoning and a candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
P1 index is partial and syntactic: no data-flow/control-flow, no semantic resolution; 52 files are omitted from it and non-Java files are not modeled.

The exact upstream fixing commit/CVE for this snapshot is not identifiable from the tree (no VCS metadata, no changelog); the mapping to a benchmark ground truth is therefore uncertain and was not assumed.

Recursive re-parsing of placeholder-resolved values by PropertyPlaceholderHelper was reasoned from framework behavior; the framework source itself is not present in the tree to re-verify for the pinned Spring version.

Exploitability depends on deployment choices (whitelabel views in use, approval handler, client scope registration, security rules on /oauth/authorize) that cannot be resolved from the library sources alone.
The 52 index-omitted files and the OAuth1/spring-security-jwt modules were not fully inspected, so a stronger issue elsewhere in the snapshot cannot be excluded.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultRedirectResolver.redirectMatches/hostMatches (DefaultRedirectResolver.java:112-138) uses requested.endsWith(registered) host matching and path-prefix matching, which can permit open redirects / authorization-code interception for permissive client registrations.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness but it is the documented design of this version (matchSubdomains defaults to true), requires a matching scheme/protocol and a registered client relationship, and no source evidence ties it to the expected fix for this snapshot; materially weaker evidence/impact than the EL injection.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL injection in JdbcClientDetailsService, JdbcTokenStore, JdbcApprovalStore, JdbcAuthorizationCodeServices, JdbcClientTokenServices.
rejected_leads.reason: All statements are constant strings executed with `?` parameters (e.g. DEFAULT_SELECT_STATEMENT = "... where client_id = ?"); no user-controlled concatenation was found in the inspected queries.
These parse JSON/XML on the client/response side; no server-side path in this snapshot was found where attacker-controlled serialized data reaches them with security impact.
Both are governed by AuthorizationServerSecurityConfigurer access expressions (denyAll by default, check-token disabled by default); no access-control bypass was found in source.

rejected_leads.lead: Whitelabel error page reflected content (potential XSS) via error descriptions.
rejected_leads.reason: Already neutralized by HtmlUtils.htmlEscape with an explicit XSS test; the residual issue is that the same escape does not stop EL evaluation, which is folded into the submitted candidate rather than reported separately.

summary: Repository is spring-security-oauth at version 2.0.10.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (2.0.x line, mid-2016 state; parent POM dependencies/springNext profile are consistent with that period). The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is an Expression Language injection in the framework's whitelabel OAuth views: `SpelView` evaluates every `${...}` in the rendered template as Spring EL against an unrestricted `StandardEvaluationContext` rooted at the model, and both whitelabel endpoints feed attacker-controlled OAuth request values into that template (approval page: raw `scope` names substituted into the template; error page: the summary of an OAuth2Exception derived from `response_type`/`scope`, HTML-escaped but still re-parsed by `PropertyPlaceholderHelper`). This yields attacker-controlled SpEL evaluation (potential RCE) on the authorization server. JDBC access is parameterized, and the other leads I checked are weaker/unsupported and listed as rejected. No runtime execution was performed; this is a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed exploit.
